idea: Harrison's chronometer lettered as a cartouche in engraved copperplate: 'H4' large, beneath it 'It kept time at sea. The Board kept it for nineteen years.' Ornamental scroll frame drawn in code. For anyone who has waited on a committee while being right.

Old place names in a stacked engraved-chart lettering list: 'Terra Incognita / Here Be Dragons / Mare Tenebrosum / Ultima Thule / Terra Australis Nondum Cognita', each in a different period letterform, spaced like a coastline of labels. Reads as a poem of what people didn't know.

A ship's log page in handwritten-style copperplate: 'Lat. 41°N. Wind NNW. Nothing to report. Everyone is fine. We are very lost.' with columns for Hour, Knots, Course drawn as ruled lines. Dry understatement of every real logbook.

Map-style lettering curved along a coastline-shaped line: 'The Sea of Things Not Yet Decided', set in spaced engraved capitals like an ocean label on an 18th-century chart. A quiet joke for the undecided and the dreamy.

Mercator's reasoning in a cartouche: 'Greenland is not that big. Mercator knew. He needed the straight lines.' Engraved title scroll, with a small ruled rhumb-line fan behind it drawn in code. For people who love a good honest distortion.

A lettering specimen of the 32 compass points, set in a ring of engraved caps (Tramontana, Greco, Levante, Sirocco, Ostro, Libeccio, Ponente, Maestro), centre blank. The old Mediterranean wind names read as beautiful words; nothing else is needed.

Cartouche reading 'Longitude: a problem of 1714, solved by a carpenter from Lincolnshire.' in ornate engraved caps with a banner scroll and a plain border. Rewards those who know the Harrison story and invites the question from those who don't.

Survey-sheet lettering: 'Benchmark. The one place we all agree on.' set in stamped surveyor's capitals inside a small cut-benchmark triangle-in-circle mark drawn in code. For people who love fixed points and the mild comedy of consensus.

An atlas index page, set as dense small engraved type: 'Index of places I meant to visit: Samarkand, Timbuktu, Ushuaia, Tromsø, Zanzibar, Valparaíso...' with dotted leaders and page-grid references (B4, F7, C12). Funny, personal, and wanderlust without a slogan cliche.

Old Norse and Latin voyage lettering, 'Vinland' set in a weathered blackletter-ish engraved hand with the line below in small caps: 'Named for what grew there. Disputed since.' Nods to Vinland map controversy and to anyone who likes a contested origin story.

A white-on-black ship's-chart title block: 'CHART OF THE COAST OF NOWHERE. Soundings in fathoms. Surveyed by someone who got bored.' In engraved chart caps with a ruled neat-line border and scale bar. Plausible, deadpan, fun.

Place-name palimpsest: 'Constantinople / Istanbul' set as engraved lettering, the first crossed with a ruled line, in the manner of a corrected map; beneath, small: 'Not (to) your business.' Wordplay on They Might Be Giants plus old cartographic lettering. For history and music nerds.

Sounding-chart numerals: a field of tiny hand-engraved depth numbers (3, 7, 12, 4, 19, 28, 11) scattered like a bathymetric chart, with one large engraved label in the middle: 'Shoal.' and below 'Proceed with doubt.' Mood piece for cautious optimists.

A ship's provisions list, hand-lettered: 'Biscuit. Salt pork. Rum. Lime juice. Hope. (Hope: low.)' Set in a ledger hand with ruled columns and quantities in old units. Charming, a little grim, very specific.

A cartographer's colophon: 'Engraved at London, 1768, by a man who never saw any of it.' Set in classic title-page engraved lettering with a swash flourish. For anyone who works from secondhand information and knows it.

The Prime Meridian arranged as a vertical line of engraved text: 'Greenwich — you are here, and also exactly 0°.' split in two halves, East and West, set in mirrored cartouche lettering on either side of a drawn line. Simple, clever, easy to wear.

Piri Reis-style portolan lettering: harbor names written perpendicular to the coast around an empty rectangular chart-shape, in tiny alternating-colour-faked-in-one-ink caps, with centre text 'Every port a promise.' Looks like a real portolan, reads like a shirt.

Franklin expedition ship names as an engraved plaque: 'EREBUS · TERROR · 1845' with beneath, 'Found, 2014 and 2016. Searching continues.' Respectful, factual, set in sober capitals; for polar-history readers.

Explorer's field-note scrawl in period hand: 'Day 112. The map was wrong. The river is in the other place.' With a dashed route line and a tiny drawn-in-code compass. For people who trust the ground over the plan.

A lettered scale bar as the whole design: a ruled alternating bar labelled in engraved numerals '0 — 1 — 2 — 3 miles' with the caption beneath, 'Everything is further than it looks.' Minimal, cartographic, and true on any hike.
